faq.q: Do I need to book biker-friendly campsites in advance?
faq.a: For peak summer weekends and popular routes like the NC500, Lake District, or Snowdonia, definitely book ahead. Mid-week and shoulder season you can often turn up, but having a backup plan is wise. Always book your first and last nights at minimum.

faq.q: What should I look for in a motorcycle-friendly campsite?
faq.a: Hardstanding or solid ground for bike parking, drying facilities for wet gear, flexible pricing for solo riders, and ideally some weather shelter or communal space. Security features like CCTV or dedicated bike compounds are a bonus.

faq.q: How much does camping cost for motorcycle touring in the UK?
faq.a: Basic campsites cost £10-20 per night, while sites with better facilities run £15-30. Many offer reduced hiker-biker rates. Budget an extra £5 daily for showers, laundry, and other facilities that may charge separately.

faq.q: Can I wild camp legally in the UK on a motorcycle tour?
faq.a: In Scotland, yes, under the access code if you're responsible and follow leave-no-trace principles. Dartmoor has designated wild camping areas. Elsewhere in England and Wales you technically need landowner permission, though discreet high-ground camping is often tolerated.

faq.q: What camping gear is essential for UK motorcycle touring?
faq.a: A weatherproof quick-pitch tent, three-season sleeping bag, inflatable mat with repair kit, compact gas stove, and waterproof stuff sacks. Practice packing and pitching at home before your tour to refine your system.

faq.q: Are campsites in Scotland better for bikers than England and Wales?
faq.a: Generally yes, Scottish campsites have invested heavily in biker facilities due to the popularity of routes like the NC500. They typically offer better drying rooms, hardstanding, and understanding of motorcyclists' needs, though excellent biker-friendly sites exist throughout the UK.

content:
Finding Proper Biker-Friendly Campsites: Your Guide to Two-Wheeled Wild Camping

I've pitched my tent in some absolute gems and some questionable spots over the years of touring Britain. The difference between a brilliant night under the stars and a miserable experience often comes down to choosing the right campsite. Not all campsites get motorcyclists, and I've learned the hard way which ones do and which ones treat us like second-class citizens.

Let me share what I've learned about finding and using biker-friendly campsites across the UK, because there's nothing worse than arriving knackered after 300 miles on the A9 only to find there's nowhere secure to park your bike or the ground's too soft for a sidestand.

What Actually Makes a Campsite Biker-Friendly?

It's not just about letting bikes in. I've stayed at dozens of campsites claiming to be motorcycle-friendly, and the reality varies massively. Here's what I look for every single time.

Secure Bike Parking

First thing I check is where I'm parking the bike overnight. The best biker campsites have dedicated hardstanding areas for motorcycles, often near the entrance or visible from the main facilities. I don't want my fully-loaded GS sinking into soft grass overnight, and I definitely don't want it tucked away somewhere I can't keep an eye on it.

Some of my favourite sites have actual motorcycle compounds with CCTV. Wildrose Campsite near Loch Lomond does this brilliantly, and I've never worried about my bike there. Others provide paving slabs or wooden boards you can use under your sidestand, which shows they actually think about motorcyclists.

Drying Facilities That Actually Work

If you've ridden through Scottish weather in October, you'll know exactly why this matters. I need somewhere to dry my gear, properly. Not a radiator in a toilet block that barely gets warm, but actual drying rooms with heated rails or radiators that work.

The campsites along the NC500 have upped their game massively in recent years. Most now have dedicated drying rooms after realising that sodden textiles don't magically dry overnight in a tent. Make sure you've got decent waterproofs from SportsBikeShop though, because even the best facilities won't help if your gear's not up to scratch.

Flexible Pitch Sizes and Pricing

Here's something that winds me up: campsites that charge the same for a solo biker with a small tent as they do for a family with a massive tent, awning, and car. Biker-friendly sites get this. They offer hiker-biker pitches or reduced rates for motorcyclists, recognising we take up less space and usually arrive late and leave early.

I've paid anywhere from £8 to £25 for a night's camping as a solo rider. The cheaper ones are often farm sites or community-run spots, while the pricier ones tend to have better facilities. Both can be brilliant if they understand bikers.

My Top Features at Biker-Friendly Campsites

Beyond the basics, these are the things that make me return to a campsite year after year.

Proper Washing Facilities for Gear

I don't mean laundry services, though they're nice. I mean somewhere to rinse the road grime off your bike, clean your visor properly, and maybe wash out some base layers. A tap with decent pressure and a bit of space to work is all it takes.

Some campsites near popular routes have gone the extra mile. There's a site near Bala in North Wales that has a basic bike wash area with a pressure washer available. After riding the Evo Triangle repeatedly, it's a godsend.

Social Spaces for Riders

The best biker campsites I've used have some kind of communal space. Could be a barn with picnic tables, a dedicated biker shelter, or just a fire pit area where riders naturally gather. These spaces are where you get the best route tips, hear about road closures before they're officially announced, and generally put the world to rights with other tourers.

I've learned about some of my best routes from conversations in these spaces. Someone once told me about a perfect alternative to the A82 on a Friday evening at a campsite near Fort William, saving me hours in traffic the next day.

Location, Location, Location

A biker-friendly campsite needs to be actually accessible to motorcyclists, which means being near good roads and ideally positioned for touring routes. I'm talking about sites you can use as a base for day rides or as perfect overnight stops on longer tours.

The campsites dotted around the Lake District nail this. You can stay centrally and have access to the Kirkstone Pass, Hardknott Pass, and Wrynose Pass all within an hour's ride. Same goes for sites in the Cairngorms for the A939 or places along the Island to Highlands route.

Booking and Planning: The Practical Bits

Right, let's talk about actually getting yourself sorted with a pitch.

Do You Need to Book Ahead?

Depends entirely on when and where you're going. Peak summer weekends in popular spots like the NC500, Snowdonia, or the Yorkshire Dales? Absolutely book ahead. I've been turned away from full campsites more times than I care to remember, usually when I've assumed I could just rock up.

Mid-week in shoulder season? You can often chance it, especially at smaller sites. I've done plenty of tours where I've only booked the first and last nights, leaving the middle flexible. It's brilliant for freedom but risky if you're headed somewhere popular.

Use our trip planning tool to map out campsites along your route beforehand, even if you don't book them all. At least you'll know your options.

What to Look for in Reviews

When I'm checking reviews, I specifically look for mentions from other motorcyclists. Comments about ground conditions, bike parking, and whether staff understand bikers are gold dust. General camping reviews don't always cover what we need to know.

Red flags include mentions of bikes being sent to overflow areas far from facilities, complaints about nowhere to dry gear, or reviews saying staff were funny about late arrivals. We often arrive later than car campers because we're covering bigger distances.

The difference between a decent campsite and a brilliant biker-friendly one is whether they understand how motorcyclists actually tour. Look for places where other riders recommend them specifically for biking, not just general camping.

Regional Recommendations and What to Expect

Let me break down what I've found in different parts of the UK, because the camping scene varies massively by region.

Scotland: The Gold Standard

Scottish campsites have really embraced motorcycle touring, probably because so many brilliant routes run through the Highlands. The NC500's popularity has driven this, but it benefits all of us.

Expect to find good biker facilities at most established sites north of Perth. The wild camping laws in Scotland also give you more flexibility, though I'd still use proper campsites most of the time for the facilities and security.

Weather's the wild card up here. I've had glorious sunshine in May and horizontal rain in August. Whatever the forecast says, assume it'll rain and pack accordingly. Sites with good shelters and drying rooms aren't a luxury in Scotland, they're essential.

Lake District and Yorkshire Dales: Busy But Brilliant

These areas get hammered with visitors, so campsites are plentiful but often busy. The upside is competition has driven quality up. Many sites now have dedicated biker areas and understand the needs of motorcycle tourers.

Book ahead here, especially for anywhere near Keswick, Ambleside, or Hawes. The roads are stunning, the camping is excellent, but everyone knows it. Mid-week visits give you more flexibility.

Wales: Hidden Gems and Varied Quality

Wales has everything from basic farm sites to premium glamping operations. The biker-friendly ones tend to be in Snowdonia or along the coast, catering to riders tackling the Welsh passes.

I've found Welsh sites to be hit and miss on biker facilities. Some are absolutely brilliant with hardstanding, others assume you're happy in a soggy field. Read reviews carefully and don't assume that being near good biking roads means they understand bikers.

South West England: Coastal Touring Base

Devon and Cornwall have loads of campsites, but they're primarily set up for beach holidays rather than motorcycle touring. You'll find biker-friendly options, but they're less common than in Scotland or the Lakes.

The advantage is the weather's generally better, so drying facilities matter less. The roads around Exmoor and Dartmoor are superb, and there are some cracking sites that work well as bases for exploring.

Wild Camping and Alternatives

Sometimes the best option isn't a campsite at all. I've had some of my best nights wild camping in Scotland or using basic bothies, but it's not for everyone and you need to know what you're doing.

Wild Camping Legally

In Scotland, you can wild camp almost anywhere under the access code, as long as you're responsible. I've pitched up in some stunning locations, always following leave-no-trace principles. Dartmoor's also legal for wild camping in certain areas.

Everywhere else in the UK, you technically need landowner permission. In practice, discreet wild camping on high ground away from habitation is rarely an issue if you're respectful, but know the legalities.

Bothies and Camping Barns

The Mountain Bothies Association maintains free shelters across the UK, mostly in Scotland and northern England. They're basic but brilliant for motorcycle touring, especially if the weather's grim. Pack light camping gear as backup because bothies can be full.

Camping barns offer a middle ground, providing basic shelter with a bit more comfort than a tent. They're scattered around the Lakes, Dales, and parts of Wales.

Essential Gear for Campsite Touring

What you pack makes or breaks a camping tour. I've refined my kit over years of trips, and here's what actually matters.

The Tent Situation

Get a tent designed for bike touring. Lightweight, quick to pitch, and able to handle British weather. I use a two-person tent even though I'm solo, because the extra space is worth the minimal weight penalty for storing gear.

Practice pitching it at home. Arriving at a campsite in fading light and drizzle is not the time to work out which pole goes where. I can get my tent up in under five minutes now, which is essential when the weather's closing in.

Sleeping System

A good sleeping bag rated for lower temperatures than you expect is crucial. British summer nights can be surprisingly cold, especially in Scotland or at altitude. I carry a three-season bag and a silk liner for flexibility.

Inflatable sleeping mats pack smaller than foam, but carry a repair kit. Puncturing your mat on day one of a week-long tour is miserable, trust me.

Cooking Kit

Keep it simple. A compact gas stove, one pot, a mug, and basic utensils. I can make a brew and heat up food, which is all you need. Campsites with facilities might have kettles and cooking areas, but don't rely on it.

Packing Smart

Waterproof bags inside your panniers or top box are essential. Everything getting soaked on day one ruins a tour. I use stuff sacks organised by type, clothing in one, camping gear in another, tools and spares in a third.

Check out our comprehensive packing checklist for more detailed guidance on what to bring.

Dealing with British Weather at Campsites

Let's be honest, camping in Britain means dealing with rain. I've camped in every month of the year, and I've been rained on in all of them.

Staying Dry and Sane

Your tent's going to get wet. Accept it. What matters is keeping you and your gear dry inside. A footprint or groundsheet under your tent stops water wicking up from below. Guy out your tent properly so rain runs off rather than pooling.

I always pack one set of dry clothes that never leaves the waterproof bag until I'm in the tent. Having something dry to change into is a massive morale boost after a wet day's riding.

Making the Most of Facilities

This is where biker-friendly campsites earn their keep. Use those drying rooms, hang your gear properly spread out so it actually dries. Get your morning brew from the facilities if it's hammering down rather than trying to cook outside.

I've spent plenty of evenings in campsite common rooms waiting out heavy rain, and it's usually where the best conversations happen.

Security and Peace of Mind

Leaving your bike and gear unattended while you're in a tent can feel sketchy, but I've rarely had issues at proper campsites.

Bike Security Basics

I always use a disc lock, even at campsites. It's a visual deterrent more than anything. If the site has a secure bike area or compound, use it. Otherwise, park where you can see your bike from your tent if possible.

Take expensive items like sat navs, phone mounts, and tank bags into your tent at night. Don't leave them as an invitation.

Gear Storage

Anything that won't fit in your tent should be locked to your bike or in locked panniers. I've never had gear stolen from a campsite, but I've heard stories. Basic precautions cost nothing.

Making the Most of Your Campsite Stay

Right, you've arrived, you've pitched up, now what?

Evening Routine

I always check my bike over in the evening. Quick visual inspection for anything loose, check tyre pressures if I've got a gauge, look for any damage from the day's ride. It's easier to spot issues in daylight than at 7am when you're trying to get on the road.

Sort your gear out for the next day. Check the forecast, plan your route, make sure everything's charged. The morning's much smoother when you've done this the night before.

Meeting Other Riders

Don't be shy about chatting to other bikers at campsites. Some of my best route recommendations and riding tips have come from campsite conversations. We're a friendly bunch generally, and most people are happy to share knowledge.

Cost Considerations and Budgeting

Camping is one of the cheapest ways to tour, but costs add up. Here's the reality of what you'll spend.

Nightly Costs

Budget £10-20 per night for basic campsites, £15-30 for better facilities. Wild camping's free but you'll likely use some campsites for facilities and security. On a week-long tour, I'll usually do 4-5 nights at campsites and maybe 1-2 wild camping.

The Hidden Costs

Showers at some campsites need pound coins. Laundry facilities cost extra. That morning bacon roll from the campsite shop adds up. Budget an extra fiver a day for these bits.

The initial investment in decent camping gear is significant, but it lasts years if you look after it. Don't cheap out on your tent or sleeping bag, they're the foundation of your comfort.

Your Action Plan for Finding Great Biker Campsites

Here's how I'd approach planning a camping tour if I were starting from scratch today.

First, plot your route roughly using our route builder. Know your rough daily distances and where you'll be each evening. Then start researching campsites in those areas, specifically looking for mentions of motorcycle-friendly facilities.

Book your first and last nights, and maybe any that are in particularly popular areas. Leave the middle flexible if you can handle that uncertainty. Make a note of backup options in case your first choice is full.

Get your gear sorted well before the tour. Test everything, practice packing your bike, do a weekend shakedown trip to iron out any issues. There's nothing worse than discovering your tent leaks or your sleeping bag's not warm enough when you're three days into a week-long tour.

Check reviews from other motorcyclists, join some touring forums or groups, and ask for recommendations. The biking community is brilliant at sharing knowledge about which campsites are actually good for us.

Finally, embrace the adventure. Camping tours aren't about luxury, they're about freedom, incredible riding, and sleeping under the stars after a brilliant day on the bike. The best biker-friendly campsites understand this and make it all possible. Now get out there and find your favourites.
